hints: Focus on how ion charge changes electron count, a positive ion has lost electrons and a negative ion has gained them.
Sodium has atomic number 11, so a neutral Na atom has 11 electrons, but $\text{Na}^+$ has lost one electron to leave 10.
Add up the electrons for three nitrogen atoms and then remember to add one more for the 1- charge on $\text{N}_3^-$.
walkthrough:
**Find electrons in the sodium ion**

Sodium has atomic number 11, so a neutral Na atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons. To form $\text{Na}^+$, it loses one electron.

Calculation rule:
$$\text{electrons in } \text{Na}^+ = 11 - 1 = 10$$

**Find electrons in the azide ion**

Nitrogen has atomic number 7, so each neutral N atom has 7 electrons. The azide group contains three N atoms, giving $3 \times 7 = 21$ electrons, then the 1- charge means one extra electron is gained.

Calculation rule:
$$\text{electrons in } \text{N}_3^- = (3 \times 7) + 1 = 22$$

**Match to the table**

Sodium ion has 10 electrons and azide ion has 22 electrons. That combination is isoelectronic with neon and is very stable, which is why $\text{Na}^+$ forms so readily.

options.A: Sodium ion with 10 is correct, but 20 for azide is wrong. This counts only $3 \times 7 = 21$ minus one, or simply forgets the extra electron for the 1- charge. Remember negative means add electrons.
options.B: This is correct. $\text{Na}^+$ has $11 - 1 = 10$ electrons and $\text{N}_3^-$ has $(3 \times 7) + 1 = 22$ electrons. Both counts correctly allow for electrons lost and gained.
options.C: Both are wrong in the same way. 12 uses the mass-related confusion or adds an electron instead of removing one for Na, and 20 misses the extra electron on the azide ion. Positive ions lose electrons, negative ions gain them.
options.D: Azide ion with 22 is correct, but 12 for sodium is wrong. This uses 11 + 1 instead of 11 - 1, treating $\text{Na}^+$ as if it gained an electron. A 1+ ion has one fewer electron than its atom.
